Yes. The subtext generally enriches the story rather than feeling forced. Miss Emily’s scrutiny of Denise’s torn blouse conveys class judgment without an explicit insult, while sliding her the tasting spoon quietly signals respect and a willingness to surrender control. The house, jars, and gifts likewise make the affluent household a setting where affection is communicated through objects and exacting standards rather than tenderness.

Occasionally, the narration explains these meanings quite directly—especially Denise’s interpretation of the above-market loan interest—leaving less room for inference. Even so, the underlying tensions between generosity, control, dignity, and belonging feel grounded in the characters.
